education.role: A classic focal flower — large, open head that anchors the eye. Most designs want 3–5 focal blooms placed through the piece, not in a row.
education.designTip: Vary the depth: recess one rose and lift another so the design reads as three-dimensional rather than flat.
education.conditioning: Strip lower foliage, remove guard petals, re-cut at 45° and rest in cool water for at least 2 hours before designing.

education.role: A statement focal with a short season (May–June in the UK). Its size means one peony can do the work of two roses.
education.designTip: Because peonies open dramatically, design with their final open size in mind, not their bud size.
education.conditioning: Buy in "marshmallow" stage — soft bud. Opens fast in warm water; hold cold to slow it.

education.role: A secondary flower: smaller layered heads that support the focal blooms and add petal texture between them.
education.designTip: Cluster ranunculus in odd-numbered groups near a focal rose to build a "moment" rather than scattering them evenly.
education.conditioning: Hollow, delicate stems — cut cleanly and avoid crushing. Wire the head for bouquet work if the neck is soft.

education.role: A workhorse secondary flower — ruffled, rose-like blooms plus buds on one branching stem, so it fills and softens at once.
education.designTip: Use the budded tips at the edges of a design to soften the outline — a hard outline is the most common student mistake.
education.conditioning: Snap off spent lower blooms; each stem offers multiple usable flower heads.

education.role: Budget mass flower with a modern comeback. Dense ruffled heads add texture and stretch a budget without reading as cheap when clustered.
education.designTip: Cluster 3–5 tightly at one depth so they read as one lush textural mass, the contemporary way to use them.
education.conditioning: Cut between nodes — cutting on a node blocks water uptake.

education.role: A mass flower: one head covers real area fast. Great for establishing the body of a design before placing focals.
education.designTip: Recess hydrangea deep in the design as a "pillow" that supports and visually lifts the flowers placed above it.
education.conditioning: Drinks through its petals — mist it, and submerge wilted heads in cool water for 30 minutes to revive.

education.role: A line flower: tall spires that create the skeleton and movement of a design and lead the eye upward or outward.
education.designTip: Place line flowers first to set the height and width of the design; everything else works inside that frame.
education.conditioning: Hollow stems — fill with water and plug with cotton wool for large-scale work, or just keep water deep.

education.role: A filler: airy clouds of tiny blooms that occupy space between flowers, soften transitions, and add air to a design.
education.designTip: Let filler float slightly higher than the flowers around it to create a soft, airy halo rather than packing it tight.
education.conditioning: Ethylene-sensitive — keep away from ripening fruit. A little goes a long way.

education.role: Foundation foliage: rounded silver leaves establish the base, shape, and colour temperature of the design before any flower is placed.
education.designTip: Build your foliage skeleton first: it defines the final silhouette and means you use fewer (expensive) flowers.
education.conditioning: Woody stems — cut at a steep angle. Scent is a signature; some clients love it, some don't. Ask.

education.role: Line foliage: long arching stems that extend the silhouette, add movement, and trail beautifully from bouquets and compotes.
education.designTip: Let one or two stems arc well beyond the outline; controlled "escapes" create rhythm and stop a design feeling like a ball.
education.conditioning: Extremely long-lasting — often outlives the flowers twice over.

education.role: A textural filler: feathery plumes that add softness and a sense of movement between firmer flower forms.
education.designTip: Contrast textures deliberately: feathery astilbe against a smooth rose makes both read more strongly.
education.conditioning: Thirsty and quick to droop — condition in deep water and design last.

education.role: The classic base foliage: flat, triangular serrated fronds that skirt a design, cover mechanics, and frame the flowers from beneath.
education.designTip: Lay leatherleaf flat under the bouquet base with tips pointing outward — it defines the outline and hides every stem end.
education.conditioning: Extremely long-lasting and robust — often the last thing standing. Store cool and dry.

education.role: A statement focal: a large, geometric ball of layered petals that anchors autumn designs the way a peony anchors summer ones.
education.designTip: One dahlia can carry a whole side of an arrangement — place it slightly off-centre and build texture around it.
education.conditioning: Thirsty and bruise-prone — cut in the cool of the day, sear or deep-water, and handle the petals as little as possible.

education.role: A clean, graphic focal — a single flat disc of radiating petals that brings a modern, cheerful note and a strong circular form.
education.designTip: Gerbera reads as a bold dot: use odd numbers and vary the heights so they punctuate rather than polka-dot the design.
education.conditioning: Hollow, floppy stems — use a gerbera straw or shallow water, and keep them upright; the heads droop otherwise.

education.role: A large, fragrant star-shaped focal that opens over days — one stem carries several blooms and buds, giving height and drama.
education.designTip: Use the open bloom as the focal and let the buds extend the line — never strip them; they are half the flower.
education.conditioning: Remove the pollen-bearing anthers to prevent staining. Buds open in sequence, extending vase life.

education.role: A tall line flower: a dense spike of dragon-mouth florets that opens from the bottom up, giving height, movement and a soft column of colour.
education.designTip: Place line flowers first to set the height and width; let a snapdragon curve rather than forcing it straight.
education.conditioning: Strongly photo-tropic — it bends toward light, so store upright. Keep water clean and re-cut; the tips keep growing.

education.role: A soft, clove-scented spike that adds mass, colour and fragrance while filling the mid-body of a design.
education.designTip: Stock brings scent and body; cluster a few for a soft column of colour rather than dotting single stems.
education.conditioning: Woody stems foul water fast — strip lower leaves, use clean water and flower food, and re-cut often.

education.role: A big, bold, cheerful focal with a strong dark centre — the anchor of rustic and late-summer designs.
education.designTip: Because the head is so large and the centre so dark, give a sunflower space; crowding it kills its impact.
education.conditioning: Heavy heads on thick stems — support them, keep water deep, and expect them to drink a lot.

education.role: A long-lasting round focal — dense, layered petals form a full dome that reads as a bold, structured bloom and holds its shape for weeks.
education.designTip: Its perfect dome can look static — set it at varied depths and pair with looser textures so it grounds the design without flattening it.
education.conditioning: One of the hardiest cut flowers: re-cut, strip the lower foliage, and it will outlast almost everything else in the arrangement.

education.role: A trailing textural line — long, tassel-like ropes of tiny florets add movement, drape and a wild, garden-gathered feel.
education.designTip: Let it spill over the edge of a bouquet or arch to break a tight outline; a few strands do a lot.
education.conditioning: Woody-stemmed and thirsty; give it a deep drink and it lasts well. The tassels shed a little — condition over a bin.

education.role: A soft, feathery statement plume — dried and airy, it brings height, neutral colour and a bohemian, textural softness.
education.designTip: Use sparingly for scale and negative space; one or two plumes read as intentional, a bunch reads as a broom.
education.conditioning: Dried, so no water needed; a light mist of hairspray reduces shedding. Handle gently — the plumes bruise and fluff.

education.role: A delicate domed secondary — a pincushion of tiny florets on a wiry stem that adds airy detail and a cottage-garden charm.
education.designTip: Float it on longer stems above the mass so the heads bob and add lightness and movement.
education.conditioning: Thin, wiry stems drink fast — keep the water topped up. The blooms are fragile; handle by the stem.

education.role: A trailing succulent — strands of round, bead-like leaves cascade downward, adding a modern, sculptural line of green.
education.designTip: Reserve it for the trailing edge of a bouquet or an elevated arrangement where it can hang and catch the light.
education.conditioning: Succulent and forgiving out of water for short spells; mist lightly. The strands snap, so drape rather than bend them.

education.role: A slender line flower — a tapering spike of tiny florets that opens from the base up, giving height, rhythm and a soft vertical accent.
education.designTip: Place the spikes early to set the height and let them lean naturally; they draw the eye upward and outward.
education.conditioning: Keep the water clean and re-cut; strip the lower leaves. The spikes keep growing and curving toward light — store upright.
